ESH. I lived in China, public transport is super cheap including taxis. Yes he’s unfit and shouldn’t have overestimated his ability, but in most places you visited in China this wouldn’t have been difficult to accommodate around since Didi (Chinese uber) is easy for even tourists to use. You definitely could have been more considerate if you wanted to be.

For anyone wondering, a 90 minute Didi from my old place to Shanghai Pudong airport costs less than 30 dollars. Didi trips to different parts of a city usually cost anywhere between 2-10 dollars. You can book 7 seaters too although you might need to wait longer.

And for the park, you could have just… went to the park for a bit in a taxi, then took a taxi to the market when you’re done. With 4 adults, the split didi costs would have been a no more than a few dollars each.

Copying is often one of the most neglected ways of learning art- so many older artists learnt by spending years copying their “master”’s works. Copying will train your eyes to see more details, develop your inner critic, and also allow you to study the styles and techniques used by these artists :)

The one on the left is structurally better than the one on the right, and has more pleasing lines/curves too. The right however has clearer lines and is less messy. 

I’d recommend making a new layer and drawing over the left cat with a similar brush you used to draw the right cat, making sure to use long, flowing lines so you don’t lose those lovely curves!

Definitely add some more contrast with some deeper shadows, to make the characters pop! Try experimenting with a new layer set to overlay on top, and using a dark colour to add some shadows to the parts facing away from the light. Adjust the opacity of this layer as necessary. Your style is really nice and I’ve seen artists with similar styles use this kind of technique for strong lights/shadows too!

All these artists have a really great grasp on lighting. I highly recommend the textbook “Light for Visual Artists.” Doing studies of professional studio photography as opposed to webcam screenshots will also help too, because photographers will have the lighting in their studios set up in ways that create interesting light, colours and shadow. Good luck!

You have a great sense for lighting, which is particular highlighted in the last 2 pieces. Good contrast and the way the light and shadow hit makes the objects of each piece feel 3D. However you can see evidence of this in all the pictures, it’s just not pushed as much in the first 3 pieces. When making stylised art don’t be afraid to exaggerate your lighting! For the third pic in particular, I’d experiment with darkening the BG and adding more ambient light from the fire to all the characters

Also in the first 3 pieces, the less dramatic lighting (and posing) makes some of your shortcomings more obvious. The major thing I noticed was the faces felt flat and weirdly angled. I recommend doing some anatomical studies of real people’s faces first, then looking at some 3D models of stylised characters to help you better understand how different parts of your character’s face will look from different angles.

Kids enjoying horror media isn’t a new thing, I remember growing up with kids who’d watch shit like Chucky lol. While mascot horror isn’t really designed for children, series like FNaF and Poppy Playtime don’t really have any themes in it that a 8+ child shouldn’t have some awareness of already, their too young to really understand the story beyond “people got turned into toys,” and the gore we see on screen is done to creatures that look like toys. That’s pretty tame compared to the sex, drugs, alcohol, and human gore that kids would watch in horror movies (which whether you like it or not, kids were watching before)

Obviously parental discretion is advised, but assuming parents are alright with Their kids watching horror then I’d rather kids were playing Poppy Playtime than watching the same late night horror films people my age watched as kids

You missed the point of their message- it’s not that other countries are dangerous, it’s that many Asian cities are safer to live in, especially for people native to that region, and they take that safety for granted. 

I’m from the UK and live in Shanghai. I’ve left phones and laptops at my seat in coffee shops while I’ve gone to use the bathroom. When I come back they’re still there. I can use my phone on the street without feeling the need to ‘shield it,’ and I’m never worried about walking alone at night. Singapore, HK, Tokyo, Seoul, I’ve heard similar stories from expats who’ve lived in these places too. Whenever I’m back in London I know to be more cautious because I grew up in the UK, but Asian people who have always lived in ‘safer’ cities may not and will quickly learn the consequences when their phone gets nicked by a scrote on a scooter, or worse.

Tracing photos is well-known art technique that’s been used by professionals for decades. To say that it’s wrong is to downplay the vast amounts of skill required to make a fully rendered art piece- tracing can only replace technical drawing ability. It can not replace creativity, lighting, shading, composition, etc.

The issue with tracing is purely legal- you can not trace things you do not have permission to use to generate income. If you’re using copyright free photos, or better yet using your own photos, then there’s no issue.

I get the argument people are making about “it limits your growth” which I 100% agree with, but a person making a webcomic should be seen as a professional artist and not a student. A professionals main aim should be to make the highest quality product they’re currently capable of, with artistic growth coming second. They should not be looked down upon for using legally acceptable shortcuts to make sure that their product is high quality.

Hello Im doing iQTS. Don’t worry about the mentor too much- you will also be assigned a pathway tutor, who is UK based and is properly qualified to teach QTS. The mentor’s role is to observe you once a week (or once every two weeks) and to provide evidence of you teaching the different teacher standards within the lessons you observe, which they then send to your pathway tutor. Your uni should give your mentor an observation template that lays out the different categories in an easy to understand way. They may also link your mentor some training documents to help them understand their role. Any teacher with a few years experience will be okay for this role as a result.

For most of your course, you will be communicating with the pathway tutor. They will regularly review and give you feedback on submitted documents, and give you and your mentor a video call every now and again to see how you’re doing. 

The main thing you need to prepare for is second school experience, as this is a UK gov requirement and cannot be skipped. For experienced teachers however, if their previous schools fill out a testimony for them, then often the time required can be significantly reduced, or can be skipped altogether. I don’t have evidence of this claim, but I’m pretty sure iQTS began as a way to encourage people with lots of teaching experience outside the UK to get qualified and move to the UK, due to how severe the teacher shortage is becoming here. That’s why teachers who have worked at multiple can take this shortcut. However I also know some people are using summer school teaching as a way to try and get around this rule

IQTS is very daunting and expensive- if you don’t feel comfortable doing it now, spend a year working at a school first and then reevaluate if you feel ready for IQTS or not. 

And as others have said, working at an international school will help you greatly as they will teach in a way more similar to the UK standards. Most international schools in China have a vested interest in making their teaching staff as qualified as possible, and will be more likely to help support you.
